title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: Kitty got to know Madame Stahl too, and this acquaintance, together with her friendship with Varenka, did more than influence her — it eased the distress she had been carrying. She found that comfort in a whole new world being opened to her through this meeting, a world with nothing in common with her past — a lofty, noble world from whose height she could look back on her past calmly. It was revealed to her that besides the instinctive life she had been giving herself up to until then, there was a spiritual life. This life was disclosed in religion, but a religion with nothing in common with the one Kitty had known since childhood, the one expressed in litanies and all-night services at the Widow's Home, where one could meet one's friends, or in memorizing Slavonic texts with the priest. This was a high, mysterious religion bound up with a whole sequence of noble thoughts and feelings — something one could do more than simply believe because told to; something one could love.

Kitty did not arrive at all this through words. Madame Stahl spoke to Kitty as one speaks to a charming child whom one watches with pleasure, the way one looks at a memory of one's own youth; only once, in passing, did she say that in all human sorrows nothing brings comfort but love and faith, and that in the light of Christ's compassion for us no sorrow is small — and at once she turned to other matters. But in every gesture of Madame Stahl, in every word, in every heavenly — as Kitty called it — look, and above all in the whole story of her life, which she heard from Varenka, Kitty recognized that something "important" of which, until now, she had known nothing.

Yet, elevated as Madame Stahl's character was, touching as her story was, and exalted and moving as her speech was, Kitty couldn't help noticing certain traits in her that bothered her. She noticed that when asked about her family, Madame Stahl had smiled with contempt, which did not fit with Christian meekness. She noticed too that when a Catholic priest had been with her, Madame Stahl had carefully kept her face in the shadow of the lamp-shade and had smiled in a peculiar way. Trivial as these two observations were, they unsettled Kitty, and she began to have her doubts about Madame Stahl. But Varenka, on the other hand — alone in the world, without friends or relations, asking nothing, regretting nothing — was exactly the kind of perfection Kitty hardly dared dream of. In Varenka she saw clearly that one had only to forget oneself and love others and one would be calm, happy, and noble. And that was what Kitty longed to be. Now that she could see plainly what was _the most important_, Kitty was not content with merely admiring it; she at once gave herself, with her whole soul, to the new life opening up before her. From Varenka's stories about Madame Stahl and other people she mentioned, Kitty had already drawn up the plan of her own future. She would, like Madame Stahl's niece Aline, of whom Varenka had told her a great deal, seek out the suffering wherever she happened to be living, help them as much as she could, give them the Gospel, read the Gospel to the sick, to criminals, to the dying. The idea of reading the Gospel to criminals, as Aline did, especially fascinated Kitty. But all this stayed secret; she did not speak of it either to her mother or to Varenka.

While she waited for the time when she could carry out her plans on a large scale, however, Kitty even now, at the springs where there were so many sick and unhappy people, easily found chances to practice her new principles in the same way Varenka did.

At first the princess noticed nothing beyond the fact that Kitty was under the strong influence of her _engouement_, as she called it, for Madame Stahl, and still more for Varenka. She saw that Kitty did not just imitate Varenka in her behavior, but unconsciously imitated her way of walking, of talking, of blinking her eyes. But later the princess began to see that, apart from this hero-worship, some real spiritual change was taking place in her daughter.

The princess saw that in the evenings Kitty read a French testament Madame Stahl had given her — something she had never done before; that she avoided her social acquaintances and spent her time with the sick people under Varenka's care, and especially with one poor family, that of a sick painter named Petrov. Kitty was unmistakably proud of playing the part of sister of mercy in that family. All of which was well enough, and the princess had nothing against it, the more so as Petrov's wife was a perfectly decent woman and the German princess, noticing Kitty's devotion, praised her and called her an angel of consolation. All of which would have been fine, if there hadn't been so much excess in it. But the princess could see that her daughter was rushing into extremes, and so she said so to her.
"_Il ne faut jamais rien outrer_," she told her.

Her daughter said nothing in reply; in her heart she was thinking that one couldn't really speak of excess where Christianity was concerned. What excess could there be in practicing a teaching that told you to turn the other cheek when struck, and to hand over your cloak if your coat were taken? But the princess didn't like this excess, and she liked even less the fact that she could feel her daughter was unwilling to open all of her heart to her. Kitty did indeed hide her new views and feelings from her mother. She hid them not because she didn't respect or love her mother, but simply because her mother was her mother. She would have shown them to anyone before her own mother.
"How is it Anna Pavlovna hasn't been to see us for so long?" the princess remarked one day of Madame Petrova. "I've asked her, but she seems put out about something."
"No, I haven't noticed it, maman," said Kitty, flushing hotly.
"Is it long since you went to see them?"
"We're planning a trip to the mountains tomorrow," Kitty answered.
"Well, you can go," the princess said, watching her daughter's embarrassed face and trying to work out what was behind that embarrassment.
That day Varenka came to dinner and reported that Anna Pavlovna had changed her mind and dropped the plan for the next day. And the princess noticed once again that Kitty colored.
"Kitty, haven't you fallen out with the Petrovs about something?" the princess asked when they were alone together. "Why has she stopped sending the children, and stopped coming herself?"

Kitty answered that nothing had happened between them, and that she couldn't say why Anna Pavlovna seemed displeased with her. Kitty answered with complete honesty. She didn't know the reason for the change in Anna Pavlovna, but she could guess at it. She could guess at something she could not tell her mother, something she could not even put into words to herself. It was one of those things one knows but can never say aloud, even to oneself, because to be wrong about it would be too dreadful and too shameful.

Again and again she went over in her memory everything that had happened with that family. She remembered the simple delight on Anna Pavlovna's round, good-humored face when they met; she remembered their quiet councils about the invalid, their little plots to draw him away from the work that was forbidden him and to get him out of doors; the devotion of the youngest boy, who used to call her "my Kitty" and would not go to bed without her. How nice it all had been! Then she pictured Petrov's thin, terribly thin figure, his long neck, the brown coat, the scant curly hair, the questioning blue eyes that had been so frightening to her at first, and his painful attempts to seem hearty and lively in her presence. She remembered the effort she had made at first to overcome the revulsion she felt for him, as for all consumptives, and the trouble it had cost her just to find things to say to him. She remembered the timid, softened way he looked at her, and the strange mix of pity, awkwardness, and later of a sense of her own goodness, that the look had stirred in her. How nice it all had been! But all that was before. Now, a few days ago, everything had suddenly soured. Anna Pavlovna had greeted Kitty with a forced cordiality, and had been watching her and her husband nonstop.
Could that touching pleasure he showed when she came near really be the cause of Anna Pavlovna's coldness?

"Yes," she thought it through, "there was something unnatural in Anna Pavlovna, something utterly unlike her good nature, when she said angrily the day before yesterday, 'There — he'll keep waiting for you; he wouldn't drink his coffee without you, even though he's grown so dreadfully weak.'"

"Yes, perhaps she didn't like it either when I gave him the rug. It was such a simple thing, but he took it so awkwardly, and went on and on thanking me, until I felt awkward myself. And then that portrait of me he did so well. And most of all that look of confusion and tenderness! Yes, yes, that's it!" Kitty repeated to herself in horror. "No, it can't be, it mustn't be! He's so much to be pitied!" she said to herself a moment later.
This doubt poisoned the charm of her new life.
